I don’t know. The upper deck had been showing dark on the screen; it had been like that for a few days. I told the garage. Everyone tells them; nobody looks.
Why didn’t the upper deck camera record?
I watch the road. The upper deck doesn’t even show in the mirror.

The lad in the red cap. He was drunk when he got on; he looked upstairs, muttered something and stayed downstairs. He got off a few stops later, I think; I’m not sure. I can’t count how many people get off.
Do you remember Kieran Doyle?

It was raining; the bus was half empty. From Bricklayers, the hospital, then a few more stops… A woman screamed upstairs and I hit the button. I stopped at Canal Bridge and opened the doors. That’s the rule; I can’t keep anyone inside.
Would you describe that journey?
“I can’t keep anyone inside.”
Someone shot out of the back door. Hooded, a bag on their back. I saw them in the mirror for a second; no face. They vanished into the rain.
Who got off the bus?
Adebayo Bello — interview

HOSPITAL NOTIFICATION — OWEN MARSH

St. Clement Hospital, 9 February 2029.

Subject: A shortfall of 14 ampoules of morphine in the night store drug cabinet over January.
Reported by: O. Marsh (porter), via supervisor H. Shaw.
Basis: count sheets submitted by H. Shaw; the shortfalls coinciding with Carter’s shifts.
Carter’s statement: “I never opened the cabinet; I don’t have a key.”
Decision: Dismissal on grounds of loss of trust. No police complaint was made.

Note: The cabinet’s card lock is to be renewed in March; an access log has been kept since February.
DISCIPLINARY RECORD — LIAM CARTER

Helen Shaw was arrested for incitement and drug theft. The cabinet access log and Owen’s unsent draft became the backbone of the file. Liam Carter’s dismissal in February was reversed; by then he was on trial for a different crime.
No connection between Kieran and Liam was found; the charge fell. Helen Shaw went on working at the hospital; a week later the fax noted a new count shortfall.
Liam was tried as the sole culprit. Helen Shaw stayed at the hospital; a week later a new count shortfall was reported in the night store.
What ‘someone had told’ Liam that night remained open in the file.
Suspicion directed at the driver drew a reaction from the union; the branch issued a letter of apology.
Kieran Doyle was taken into custody; the card statement in his lawyer’s hands collapsed the file at the first hearing. No one looked for the owner of the ·4417 card.
Liam Carter was arrested for the murder of Owen Marsh. At trial he described Helen Shaw’s phone call; his defence put forward the incitement as a mitigating factor.
The file remained unsolved. The count shortfalls at the hospital continued.

A scuffle between two men outside a kebab shop. Parties: Owen Marsh (38) and Kieran Doyle (24). Cause: an argument over the queue. Doyle mildly under the influence of alcohol. No injuries. The parties were warned and released; neither wished to press charges.

Officer’s note: “Marsh was calm; he said ‘I’m late for my shift’ and walked to the hospital.”

With the victim’s supervisor.
You’d need to speak to the hospital management about that.

There was an incident in February. Count shortfalls in the drug cabinet. Owen noticed someone and came to me; I took it to management. A porter called Liam Carter was dismissed. Liam never forgave Owen for it.
Clasped her hands on the table.
Was there anyone who had a problem with Owen?
Meticulous. Too meticulous sometimes. He never misses a count, and doesn’t let anyone else miss one either. I can’t believe it.
Was trying to keep her voice steady.
What is Owen Marsh like?
“He never misses a count.”
Everyone knows. They worked the same shift for three years.
Would Liam have known what time Owen finished?
He left at twenty past one. He was running to catch his usual bus. The stop is right in front of the hospital.
How did his shift end that night?
Helen Shaw — interview
On Owen’s phone.
The supervisors and the night nurse in charge. There’s a card lock now. Management keeps the logs.
Who has access to the drug cabinet?
Owen had been very tired in recent weeks. He was mixing up the counts. He called me, yes; I calmed him down. I said, ‘Let’s have a look before you go to the manager.’ That’s all.
Smiled; the smile did not reach her eyes.
What did Owen want to tell you?
No. Why would I? I had a part in his dismissal; he hates me.
Have you been in contact with Liam Carter recently?
Helen Shaw — second interview
On the phone record and the access log.
…I called. To warn him. I told him Owen was going to the police again, that he’d give his name. So he’d be prepared. I didn’t tell him to do anything to him. Never.
Her voice shook for the first time.
Would you describe the call on the evening of 15 March?
The card is mine, yes. Someone else may have used it. I won’t say anything more until my lawyer gets here.
The cabinet logs show your card.
Helen Shaw — third interview
Because… Owen was wrong. I… I want my lawyer.
Looked at the paper on the table, stood up, sat down again.
According to Owen’s draft, it wasn’t Liam. Why didn’t you tell Liam that?

HOSPITAL INFORMATION NOTE — OWEN MARSH
Statement of the young man involved in the fight.
It’s the only bus home! I got on, saw him upstairs, said something and stayed downstairs. Then I got off. I didn’t touch him.
Why did you get on the same bus?
I don’t know, mate; I was just going home.
At the kebab shop, over the queue. He bumped my shoulder, and I said whatever came into my head. Two punches, that’s it. Then the police came and split us up.
Folded his arms.
What happened with Owen Marsh?
“I didn’t touch him.”
Kieran Doyle — interview
I don’t know, some stop. I was out of it. I was going the wrong way anyway; I got off and got another bus on the other side. To my brother’s place.
Screwed up his face trying to remember.

On the card statement.
Dun Cow… yes! I got off there, crossed over and got on the N63. See, I told you. When he was hit I was on another bus, right?
Relaxed, then his eyes filled.
Shall we read this statement together?
Someone was sitting at the back, two rows behind Owen. In a hood. Owen was looking at him; he seemed annoyed. I was caught up in my own stuff.

TIDECARD STATEMENT — KIERAN DOYLE
Statement of the former porter.
I don’t know about that. I don’t work there any more.
No. I didn’t even have a key to that cabinet. But the sheets showed my shift, that’s all. Nobody listened.
Did you take the morphine?
I was at home, in Walworth. On my own. I didn’t take the bus; look at my Tidecard if you like, it hasn’t been tapped since yesterday.
Where were you last night?
We worked side by side for three years. Then he reported me as a thief. What do you expect me to feel? But I didn’t want anything to happen to him.
His jaw tightened.

“Look at my Tidecard.”

I have. I was at home.
Think about last night again.
I have, a cycling bag. Reflective. I used to cycle in and out; after they threw me out of the hospital that ended too. What’s that got to do with anything?

On the boarding log.

Was silent for a long time, then his voice cracked.
Would you explain this line?
A lock. A bike lock. It’s always in my bag. I didn’t know what I was doing, I swear.

Liam Carter — third interview
He got on, saw me and sat two rows in front. I said his name. He didn’t even turn round. Then… I don’t remember what happened after that. The woman screamed, and I ran.
What happened on the upper deck?
Because it was starting again. Someone told me; Owen was going to go to the police, give my name again. I was going to go to prison for something I didn’t do.
Did not say who; looked away.
Why that night? You’d kept away from him for months.
On his call with Helen Shaw.
That Owen had gone to the police again. With ‘proof’ this time. That I’d go to prison, that even she couldn’t do anything. She said, ‘I’m telling you as a favour.’ I couldn’t sleep for two days.
His eyes filled.
On the evening of 15 March Helen Shaw called you. What did she say?
Liam Carter — fourth interview
What?… No. No, she told me… She told me the exact opposite. I… Was it for that that I…
Buried his face in his hands; for a while he could not speak.
Owen was going to tell the manager that you were innocent.

At 01.48 on 17 March 2029, the driver of a Riverside Transit N219 night bus pressed the emergency button. The bus stopped at the Canal Bridge stop at 01.49.

An unconscious man was found in the back row of the upper deck: Owen Marsh (38), night porter at St. Clement Hospital. He had a severe blow to the back of the head. He was taken to hospital; his condition is serious.

The other passenger on the upper deck said she heard a scream and, when she turned round, saw a person running down the stairs. When the doors opened at the stop, someone got off through the back door and made off.

Patrol note: “It was learned that the victim had fought with a man named Kieran Doyle at a kebab shop on Old Kent Road at around 21.40 the same night, and that the incident was recorded. The driver confirmed that Doyle also boarded the same bus.”

The upper deck camera did not record.

The boarding log was anonymous, but the ·4417 card appeared in Liam’s bank transactions in the same minute. Kieran’s card statement put him on another bus at the moment of the attack. Owen’s unsent draft, the cabinet access log and Liam’s phone record pointed to Helen.

A record speaks as much through what it doesn’t capture as through what it does: only boardings are tapped, and a clean card doesn’t show a person wasn’t there. Finding who struck the blow doesn’t close the file; look at who had it struck, and why.
N219 night bus, Old Kent Road — 17 March 2029

For months, the shift supervisor Helen Shaw had been taking morphine from the hospital night store. In February she showed Owen Marsh the short count sheets and had him report Liam Carter; Liam was dismissed. When the shortfalls continued, Owen understood the truth and decided to go to the manager. On the evening of 15 March, Helen called Liam and told him Owen was going to report him to the police again. On the night of 17 March Liam boarded the N219 with his bank card, waited for Owen on the upper deck and struck him on the head with a bike lock. Owen died that afternoon. Kieran Doyle, whom he had fought with, had got off the bus before the attack.
Who struck Owen on the upper deck?
